Title: Algorithmic fandom: how generative AI is reshaping sports marketing, fan engagement, and the integrity of sport
Source title: Frontiers in Sports and Active Living
Affiliations: Victoria University Business School, Victoria University, Melbourne, Australia
Authors with affiliations: Westerbeek H., Victoria University Business School, Victoria University, Melbourne, Australia
Abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (AI) is rapidly transforming the landscape of sports marketing by enabling hyper-personalised fan engagement, real-time content delivery, and data-driven commercial strategies. Leveraging technologies such as machine learning, predictive analytics, and automated content generation, sports organisations are increasingly able to tailor fan experiences, anticipate behaviour, and optimise revenue models. While these advancements offer significant opportunities for enhancing interactivity and commercial growth, they also introduce complex ethical, psychological, and regulatory challenges. This paper critically examines the dual nature of generative AI in sports marketing, with a particular focus on consumer autonomy, data monetisation, and the influence of AI-driven personalisation on fan behaviour. Using narrative literature review approach, the paper draws on emerging research, industry cases, and interdisciplinary literature, and explores how algorithmic recommendation systems can manipulate fan decisions, reinforce digital echo chambers, and marginalise underrepresented sports. Special attention is given to the impact of AI on children and adolescents, who are particularly vulnerable to targeted content, gamification, and AI-curated betting environments. The integration of AI in gambling platforms and the commercialisation of fan data raise significant concerns around privacy, consent, and long-term wellbeing. The paper concludes by offering some implementation guidance for sport ecosystem stakeholders. It also outlines a future research agenda that calls for empirical investigations into the long-term effects of AI on fan behaviour, the development of regulatory frameworks to safeguard consumer rights, and interdisciplinary collaboration to design ethical AI systems. By identifying these critical issues, the paper aims to support a more inclusive, transparent, and integrity-focused application of AI in sport. 2025 Westerbeek.

Title: Teaching Craft Intelligence: Sovereignty Protocols for AI-Mediated Student Leadership
Affiliations: Seattle, WA, United States
Authors with affiliations: Haskell C., Seattle, WA, United States
Abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) now mediates how student leaders learn and decide, creating a speed imperative that often rewards algorithmic fluency over human judgment and intercultural accountability. This article argues student leadership programs can turn AI from a plagiarism risk into a laboratory for craft intelligence (transforming knowledge and lived experience into sound judgment in action) and deliberate stewardship, which safeguards how knowledge is created, tested, and shared. It maps four perils (e.g., inquiry collapse, context erasure, algorithmic authority, and cultural narrowing) that introduces a Trace of Agency toolkit of four sovereignty protocols to make AI-assisted decisions transparent and leadership claims auditable. © 2026 The Author(s). Title: INTRODUCTION: Why Digital Methods? Why a Feminist Lens?
Affiliations: Department of English, University of Waterloo, Canada; Feminist Digital Methods Research Cluster, Canada
Authors with affiliations: Bhandari A., Department of English, University of Waterloo, Canada; York-Bertram S., Feminist Digital Methods Research Cluster, Canada
Abstract: It is undeniable that “the digital” has transformed nearly every facet of contemporary life. From how we communicate and connect, to how we work, learn, and create, digital technologies have become embedded across wide-ranging infrastructures of daily life. Not only does the digital realm shape our social imaginaries and everyday practices, but it also conditions the very methods we as researchers use to inquire into the social world. Focusing specifically on the social sciences and humanities, digital methods—from web scraping and social network analysis to online ethnography and algorithmic curation—have become ubiquitous. Yet these methods are often adopted uncritically without sufficient attention to their political, ethical, and epistemological dimensions. © 2027 selection and editorial matter, Aparajita Bhandari and Sarah York-Bertram; individual chapters, the contributors.

Title: Conceptualizing the evolving nature of computational propaganda: a systematic literature review

Affiliations: School of Information Management, Victoria University of Wellington, Wellington, 6140, New Zealand
Authors with affiliations: Mustafa H., School of Information Management, Victoria University of Wellington, Wellington, 6140, New Zealand; Luczak-Roesch M., School of Information Management, Victoria University of Wellington, Wellington, 6140, New Zealand; Johnstone D., School of Information Management, Victoria University of Wellington, Wellington, 6140, New Zealand
Abstract: Since the 2016 U.S. election and the U.K. Brexit campaign, computational propaganda has become an important research topic in communication, political and social science. Recently, it has become clearer that computational propaganda doesn’t start from a clean slate and is not precisely bound to single issues or campaigns. Instead, computational propaganda needs to be looked at as a complex phenomenon in a global environment of co-evolving issues and events, emerging technologies, policies and legal frameworks, and social dynamics. Here, we review the literature on computational propaganda from this perspective and theorize this evolving and longitudinal nature of computational propaganda campaigns through the lens of relational dynamics. Our conceptual contribution forms the basis for a new kind of empirical research on computational propaganda that is aware of the complex interdependencies, feedback cycles and structural conditions that are elusive when focusing on individual campaigns and short time frames. © The Author(s) 2025. blob: conceptualizing the evolving nature of computational propaganda: a systematic literature review since the 2016 u.s. election and the u.k. brexit campaign, computational propaganda has become an important research topic in communication, political and social science. recently, it has become clearer that computational propaganda doesn’t start from a clean slate and is not precisely bound to single issues or campaigns. instead, computational propaganda needs to be looked at as a complex phenomenon in a global environment of co-evolving issues and events, emerging technologies, policies and legal frameworks, and social dynamics. here, we review the literature on computational propaganda from this perspective and theorize this evolving and longitudinal nature of computational propaganda campaigns through the lens of relational dynamics. our conceptual contribution forms the basis for a new kind of empirical research on computational propaganda that is aware of the complex interdependencies, feedback cycles and structural conditions that are elusive when focusing on individual campaigns and short time frames. © the author(s) 2025. published by oxford university press on behalf of the international communication association. this is an open access article distributed under the terms of the creative commons attribution-noncommercial license (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-nc/4.0/), which permits non-commercial re-use, distribution, and reproduction in any medium, provided the original work is properly cited. for commercial re-use, please contact reprints@oup.com for reprints and translation rights for reprints. all other permissions can be obtained through our rightslink service via the permissions link on the article page on our site—for further information please contact journals.permissions@oup.com. algorithmic manipulation; bots; computational propaganda; digital communication; disinformation; micro-targeted ads; platform affordances

Title: Beyond Algorithms: K-means-Driven Insights into a Technological and Educational Approach to Digital Well-being

Authors with affiliations: Fang L., Jimei University Chengyi College, Fujian, Xiamen, China; Zhang C., Jiangsu Normal University, Jiangsu, Xuzhou, China; Xu X., Philippine Normal University, Manila, Philippines; Dai W., Jimei University Chengyi College, Fujian, Xiamen, China
Abstract: Concerns about the narrowing effects of algorithmic recommendation on young people's content exposure have increased in recent years. This study aims to examine how socio-cognitive factors, usage patterns, and social network attributes jointly shape college students' perceived content diversity. Based on survey data from 392 students, we employed multiple regression models together with a K-means clustering algorithm to identify user profiles associated with higher or lower levels of content diversity. Results show that perceived diversity is not determined solely by algorithmic curation. Longer time spent on social media, higher network reciprocity, and personality traits such as openness and empathy are significant positive predictors, whereas platform diversity and most structural network attributes are not. Clustering analysis further reveals a user group characterized by high reciprocity and strong socio-cognitive traits who experience the greatest content diversity. These findings suggest that improving digital well-being requires integrating technical adjustments to recommendation systems with educational strategies that strengthen users' openness, empathy, and reciprocal engagement.  © 2025 Copyright held by the owner/author(s).

Title: Surveillance Pedagogies: Power, Monitoring, and Control in AI-Enhanced Learning Environments
Source title: Decolonizing AI Bias in Curriculum and Instructional Design
Affiliations: Tezpur University, India
Authors with affiliations: Sarkar R., Tezpur University, India
Abstract: This chapter critically examines the rise of AI-driven surveillance in education, highlighting its implications for power, equity, and pedagogy. It argues that surveillance technologies-such as automated proctoring, learning analytics, and biometric monitoring-reconfigure educational governance by embedding algorithmic authority and reducing human agency. Drawing on critical data studies, surveillance theory, and decolonial perspectives, the chapter demonstrates how these systems disproportionately impact marginalized learners, reinforce structural inequalities, and undermine privacy and democratic participation. It further interrogates surveillance pedagogies as extensions of colonial logics of classification and control. In response, the chapter proposes a decolonial and ethical AI pedagogical framework that prioritizes transparency, inclusivity, and learner agency, offering pathways toward equitable, trust-based, and participatory educational environments. © 2027 by IGI Global Scientific Publishing. Abstract: This article examines the ethical implications of big data in human resource management (HRM) practices, specifically in the areas of recruitment and selection, training and development, performance management, compensation, and employee retention. The article commences with a characterization of big data applications in HRM processes and practices, highlighting their benefits and value for the management of the workforce. It also shows how the application of big data analytics can put employees at great risk through institutional surveillance and other algorithmic manipulation practices such as profiling, coercion and control. Our theorizing advances the HRM and ethics literatures by offering a more expanded and nuanced view of the significant ethical challenges specific to individual HR practices. Additionally, our analysis brings ethics into the domain of HRM by problematizing the exploitation of employee information through digital technology for corporate gain. In so doing, it employs a moral principles framework to show how BDA - HRM practices can compromise employees' rights to privacy, confidentiality, transparency, and protection. Our analysis also raises concerns shared by both the practitioner and scholarly communities that are yet to be addressed and offers recommendations for research and practice. © 2024 Elsevier Inc.

Affiliations: Islamia University, Bahawalpur, Pakistan

Abstract: This study looks at how online hate networks, algorithmic curation, and disinformation interact to create, magnify, and legitimize Islamophobia throughout European digital spaces. The study reveals how coordinated groups and automated accounts spread misleading narratives that portray Muslim communities as cultural outsiders or security dangers by utilizing mixed methods digital ethnography, social- network analysis, and computational text mining. By encouraging sensational, divisive content, platform algorithms further strengthen these narratives and increase the exposure and reach of anti- Muslim prejudice. Additionally, the study assesses the social and political ramifications of these processes, including their effects on community- level peacebuilding efforts, minority safety, and intergroup trust. The study identifies significant gaps in platform governance and state policy by charting the digital channels by which Islamophobia proliferates. © 2026 by IGI Global Scientific Publishing. Title: Multimedia, engagement, and diffusion in alternative online communities: evidence from Spanish telegram channels
Affiliations: Department of Computer Science and Artificial Intelligence, Universidad de Granada, Granada, Spain; Facultad de Artes y Ciencias Sociales, Universidad Internacional de La Rioja, Logroño, Spain
Authors with affiliations: Gómez-Romero J., Department of Computer Science and Artificial Intelligence, Universidad de Granada, Granada, Spain; Cantón-Correa J., Facultad de Artes y Ciencias Sociales, Universidad Internacional de La Rioja, Logroño, Spain; Fajardo W., Department of Computer Science and Artificial Intelligence, Universidad de Granada, Granada, Spain; Molina-Solana M., Department of Computer Science and Artificial Intelligence, Universidad de Granada, Granada, Spain
Abstract: Multimedia content has become increasingly prominent in online communication, yet its role in shaping information diffusion in non-algorithmic platforms remains insufficiently understood. This study investigates how content format relates to message visibility and cross-channel diffusion within Spanish alternative Telegram channels. Using a longitudinal dataset of over 1.7 million messages (2019–2025), we analyze engagement through within-channel performance metrics and propagation through inter-channel forwarding networks. Building on theories of cognitive fluency, heuristic processing, and network-based diffusion, we examine the role of multimedia content in driving visibility and information spread. Our results show that multimedia messages are systematically more likely to achieve above-average visibility and to enter cross-channel diffusion circuits, even when controlling for channel-level heterogeneity. Moreover, multimedia diffusion occurs within denser and more centralized forwarding networks, suggesting that content format is associated with distinct structural pathways of amplification. These findings indicate that, in the absence of algorithmic curation, content format functions as a primary driver of both attention and diffusion. Rather than representing a purely stylistic feature, multimedia emerges as a structural component of information dynamics within alternative Telegram ecosystems. © The Author(s) 2026.

Title: Choose sustainable! How digital nudging architectures shape sustainable choices and consumer perceptions
Affiliations: Department of Economics and Business management, University of Parma, Parma, Italy
Authors with affiliations: Aiolfi S., Department of Economics and Business management, University of Parma, Parma, Italy; Bellini S., Department of Economics and Business management, University of Parma, Parma, Italy; Pellegrini D., Department of Economics and Business management, University of Parma, Parma, Italy; Bacchilega C., Department of Economics and Business management, University of Parma, Parma, Italy
Abstract: Purpose – This study aims to investigate the effectiveness of different digital nudging architectures in promoting sustainable consumer behaviour during the shopping experience. This research addresses a critical research gap by providing the first empirical comparison of theoretically grounded digital nudging models specifically designed to foster conscious shopping decisions. Design/methodology/approach – A between-subjects experimental design involving 195 participants was implemented to compare the impact of three digital nudging architectures – make together, in-sourcing and crowd-sourcing – on multiple consumer outcomes. These outcomes include engagement, perceived usefulness, willingness to pay a premium price, trust in the retailer, retailer credibility and commitment to charitable initiatives. Findings – All three digital nudging architectures elicited generally positive consumer evaluations, although with differentiated outcome profiles. The only statistically significant difference concerned the perceived relevance of the initiative, which was higher in the crowd-sourcing condition than in the make together condition. Descriptive patterns further suggest that crowd-sourcing is associated with stronger relational and engagement-oriented responses, in-sourcing with higher perceived usefulness and retailer credibility and make together with stronger purchase-related responses such as intention to buy and willingness to pay a premium. Research limitations/implications – Managerial implications are provided for designing engaging, ethically responsible digital nudges and sustainability campaigns in retail environments. Originality/value – To the best of the authors’ knowledge, this is the first empirical study to compare distinct digital nudging architectures in a sustainability context, offering a structured, theory-driven evaluation. The study advances knowledge in behavioural marketing and digital retailing by (1) offering a structured comparison of nudging architectures for sustainability goals, (2) evaluating how such interventions influence cognitive, emotional and behavioural consumer outcomes, (3) emphasising the strategic role of retailers in digital sustainability communication and (4) addressing the ethical acceptability of nudging in preserving consumer autonomy. © 2026 Simone Aiolfi, Silvia Bellini, Davide Pellegrini and Chiara Bacchilega.

Title: THE ALGORITHMIC GAZE: AI AND THE SYNTHETIC A PRIORI OF BEAUTY
Affiliations: Shri Mata Vaishno Devi University, School of Languages and Literature, Union Territory of Jammu and Kashmir, Katra, India
Authors with affiliations: Dwivedi A.V., Shri Mata Vaishno Devi University, School of Languages and Literature, Union Territory of Jammu and Kashmir, Katra, India
Abstract: This article examines the Kantian account of aesthetic judgment amid the generation and circulation of images through computational systems. Building on Immanuel Kant’s view that judgments of beauty depend on an a priori structure of reflective judgment, the paper advances two related theses. First, contemporary generative models can produce outputs that reliably elicit human experiences of beauty; yet they do so without the subjective purposiveness and intentional directedness that Kant associates with artistic genius. Their operations follow statistical inference and pattern optimization rather than reflective intention. Second, a more consequential transformation occurs at the level of reception: recommendation systems and platform feeds reorganize which forms become visible, repeatable and culturally normative, thereby shaping the dispositions through which aesthetic judgments arise. What appears beautiful is increasingly conditioned by infrastructures that predict, rank, and circulate images at scale. By placing Kant in dialogue with debates on intentionality, media theory and neuroaesthetics, and by drawing on empirical research on algorithmic curation in music streaming and social platforms, the article proposes understanding the aesthetic a priori as technogenetic— historically plastic and increasingly externalized into systems of prediction, optimization and digital mediation. Beauty, therefore, does not disappear but is judged and shared under reconfigured conditions. © 2025 Journal of Dharma:.

Title: Algorithms of Resistance and Antimacchine: A Dialogic Review about Algorithmic Agency and Creative Misuse in a Platform Society
Affiliations: Università Degli Studi di Torino, Turin, Italy
Authors with affiliations: Kratter Z., Università Degli Studi di Torino, Turin, Italy
Abstract: This dialogic review examines Tiziano Bonini and Emiliano Treré's book Algorithms of Resistance: The Everyday Fight against Platform Power alongside Antimacchine. Mancare di rispetto alla tecnologia [Anti-Machines: Disrespecting Technology] by Valentina Tanni. Bonini and Treré theorize algorithmic agency through the concepts of moral economy and everyday tactics, while Tanni addresses technological disobedience through the creative misappropriation and deconstruction of technological objects. Read together, the two works challenge representations of users just as passive subjects of platform power and show how workers, creators, activists, artists, but also ordinary users can appropriate technological systems in various ways. However, these forms of agency remain precarious: they are not equally accessible, are vulnerable to co-optation, and, above all, are often limited in scope and not sufficient to significantly transform the infrastructures they oppose. Examining examples of agency reveals the failure of a purely formal conception of private autonomy, and the subsequent need to move toward transparency, interoperability, and collective forms of governance as necessary conditions for more effective digital self-determination. © 2026 Walter de Gruyter GmbH, Berlin/Boston.

Title: Caught Between Convenience and Autonomy: Psychological Dilemmas in Consumers' Use of AI-Enabled Personalization
Affiliations: Faculty of Business and Economics, Universiti Malaya, Kuala lumpur, Malaysia; School of Management, Universiti Sains Malaysia, Penang, Malaysia
Authors with affiliations: Tiwari V., Faculty of Business and Economics, Universiti Malaya, Kuala lumpur, Malaysia, School of Management, Universiti Sains Malaysia, Penang, Malaysia
Abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) enabled personalization offers consumers greater convenience and relevance, but also generates important psychological tensions. This research examines how consumers navigate the personalization-privacy, convenience-control, and connection-isolation dilemmas that emerge in AI-mediated environments. Drawing on Self-Determination Theory, Psychological Reactance Theory, and human-AI interaction research, three complementary studies were conducted. Study 1, a 2 × 2 experiment, demonstrates that trust cues strengthen consumers' willingness to adopt AI-enabled personalization while mitigating privacy-related concerns. Study 2 shows that anthropomorphic AI enhances empathy and perceived relatedness but may also increase feelings of isolation. Study 3, using PLS-SEM and bootstrapped mediation analysis, confirms that perceived autonomy mediates the relationship between AI-enabled convenience and adoption intentions, while reduced autonomy increases psychological reactance and lowers continued usage intentions. Collectively, the findings suggest that consumer responses to AI are shaped not only by technological benefits but also by perceptions of agency, control, and social connection. By conceptualizing AI-enabled personalization as a system of interconnected psychological dilemmas organized around perceived autonomy, this research advances theory in consumer psychology and human-AI interaction while offering practical guidance for designing AI-enabled systems that support consumer autonomy, trust, and long-term engagement. © 2026 Wiley Periodicals LLC.

blob: caught between convenience and autonomy: psychological dilemmas in consumers' use of ai-enabled personalization artificial intelligence (ai) enabled personalization offers consumers greater convenience and relevance, but also generates important psychological tensions. this research examines how consumers navigate the personalization-privacy, convenience-control, and connection-isolation dilemmas that emerge in ai-mediated environments. drawing on self-determination theory, psychological reactance theory, and human-ai interaction research, three complementary studies were conducted. study 1, a 2 × 2 experiment, demonstrates that trust cues strengthen consumers' willingness to adopt ai-enabled personalization while mitigating privacy-related concerns. study 2 shows that anthropomorphic ai enhances empathy and perceived relatedness but may also increase feelings of isolation. study 3, using pls-sem and bootstrapped mediation analysis, confirms that perceived autonomy mediates the relationship between ai-enabled convenience and adoption intentions, while reduced autonomy increases psychological reactance and lowers continued usage intentions. collectively, the findings suggest that consumer responses to ai are shaped not only by technological benefits but also by perceptions of agency, control, and social connection. by conceptualizing ai-enabled personalization as a system of interconnected psychological dilemmas organized around perceived autonomy, this research advances theory in consumer psychology and human-ai interaction while offering practical guidance for designing ai-enabled systems that support consumer autonomy, trust, and long-term engagement. © 2026 wiley periodicals llc. ai personalization; artificial intelligence; consumer autonomy; consumer dilemmas; consumer trust; human-ai interaction; psychological reactance

Abstract: This chapter explores the transformation of authorship in the post-digital era, where human creativity converges with algorithmic agency and audience participation. Tracing historicalshifts from modernist notions ofthe“artist-genius”to postmodern intertextuality andcomputationalcreativity, it examines how algorithms evolve from passive tools to active co-creators. Throughtheoreticaldiscussion andcase studies on generative art, AI-assisted product design, and algorithmically curated exhibitions, the chapter highlights hybrid authorship as a relational and networked practice. Ethical, legal, and philosophical concerns ranging from intellectual property and authenticity to bias and accountability are critically analyzed. The proposed model emphasizes inclusive, collaborative, and ethically responsible creativity, offering pathways for design education, cultural production, and future research. Title: To See or Not to See: Understanding the Tensions of Algorithmic Curation for Visual Arts
Source title: 2024 ACM Conference on Fairness, Accountability, and Transparency, FAccT 2024
Affiliations: Fujitsu Research of America, United States of America, United States
Authors with affiliations: Srinivasan R., Fujitsu Research of America, United States of America, United States
Abstract: Algorithmic recommendation is one of the most popular applications of machine learning (ML) systems. While the implication of algorithmic recommendation has been studied in the context of high-stakes domains such as finance and healthcare, there has been very little focus in understanding its impacts with respect to the arts domain. Given that ML is increasingly finding place in the arts domain such as in generative arts and content analysis, in this paper, we examine the tensions of algorithmic curation in the context of visual arts. Through case studies, we describe how curatorial algorithms that are oblivious of broader socio-cultural contexts could potentially result in ethical concerns such as over-representation and misattribution, to name a few. Towards addressing some of these concerns, the paper offers design guidelines. Specifically, the paper outlines repair strategies that suggest ways 1) to engage with cultural stakeholders in building visual art curatorial algorithms, 2) to unlearn biases embedded in digital artworks and their meta-data, and 3) emphasize the need to establish regulatory norms specific to the use of ML in visual art curation. Taking cue from the process employed by artwork curators, the paper also describes how authenticity can be prioritized by re-calibrating visual art curatorial algorithms. The paper also suggest ways through which the potential of state-of-the-art ML curatorial algorithms can be re-imagined towards empowering the audience of artworks. We hope the insights presented in the paper spark interdisciplinary discussions and pave way for fostering reformation in algorithmic curation of visual arts.  © 2024 ACM.

blob: to see or not to see: understanding the tensions of algorithmic curation for visual arts algorithmic recommendation is one of the most popular applications of machine learning (ml) systems. while the implication of algorithmic recommendation has been studied in the context of high-stakes domains such as finance and healthcare, there has been very little focus in understanding its impacts with respect to the arts domain. given that ml is increasingly finding place in the arts domain such as in generative arts and content analysis, in this paper, we examine the tensions of algorithmic curation in the context of visual arts. through case studies, we describe how curatorial algorithms that are oblivious of broader socio-cultural contexts could potentially result in ethical concerns such as over-representation and misattribution, to name a few. towards addressing some of these concerns, the paper offers design guidelines. specifically, the paper outlines repair strategies that suggest ways 1) to engage with cultural stakeholders in building visual art curatorial algorithms, 2) to unlearn biases embedded in digital artworks and their meta-data, and 3) emphasize the need to establish regulatory norms specific to the use of ml in visual art curation. taking cue from the process employed by artwork curators, the paper also describes how authenticity can be prioritized by re-calibrating visual art curatorial algorithms. the paper also suggest ways through which the potential of state-of-the-art ml curatorial algorithms can be re-imagined towards empowering the audience of artworks. we hope the insights presented in the paper spark interdisciplinary discussions and pave way for fostering reformation in algorithmic curation of visual arts.  © 2024 acm. algorithmic recommendation; Title: THE EPISTEMIC CRISIS OF AUDIOVISUAL EVIDENCE IN THE AGE OF DEEPFAKES: A PROCEDURAL-NORMATIVE FRAMEWORK FOR AUTHENTICATION AND JUDICIAL EVALUATION; [LA CRISIS EPISTEMICA DE LA PRUEBA AUDIOVISUAL EN LA ERA DE LOS DEEPFAKES: MARCO PROCESAL-NORMATIVO PARA LA AUTENTICACIÓN Y VALORACIÓN JUDICIAL]
Affiliations: Universidad Privada del Norte, Peru
Authors with affiliations: Ramos-Zaga F., Universidad Privada del Norte, Peru
Abstract: The proliferation of audiovisual content manipulated through artificial intelligence represents an unprecedented challenge to the epistemic function of contemporary judicial proceedings. This research critically analyzes the normative and dogmatic frameworks for authentication and evaluation of evidence in common law and civil law systems, identifying the structural inadequacies that deepfakes reveal in both legal traditions. Through a trans-systemic comparative analysis, the erosion of traditional criteria of authenticity, relevance, and probative value is examined, alongside the cognitive and epistemological impacts that algorithmic manipulation generates on judges, expert witnesses, and testimonial evidence. Emerging regulatory strategies in the European Union and the United States are evaluated, particularly Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 and its potential incorporation into procedural mechanisms of judicial control. As a result, a hybrid model of comprehensive control is proposed, articulating a phase of technical-legal authentication based on algorithmic traceability and digital chain of custody, followed by a stage of rational evaluation grounded in expanded judicial sound criticism. This procedural framework seeks to reestablish the epistemic legitimacy of the judicial system through the integration of technological reliability criteria and argumentative reasonableness, thereby guaranteeing effective judicial protection in contexts of high digital complexity. © 2026, Universidade do Estado do Rio de Janeiro. Title: The social cyborg consumer: posthumanist framework for socio-technical consumer behavior
Affiliations: University of Las Palmas de Gran Canaria, Las Palmas de Gran Canaria, Spain
Authors with affiliations: William E., University of Las Palmas de Gran Canaria, Las Palmas de Gran Canaria, Spain
Abstract: Contemporary consumers increasingly function as human–machine hybrids, challenging traditional consumer behavior models that assume a single, bounded human decision-maker. This conceptual paper introduces the Social Cyborg Consumer framework, which integrates posthumanist philosophy of technology with mainstream consumer behavior research and behavioral economics to reconceptualize consumer choice as co-produced by human cognition and machine intelligence. Building on classical decision models and digital consumer behavior research, we argue that extant theories often treat AI, algorithms, and platforms as external influences rather than as constituents of the consumer’s own decision system. We develop six socio-technical “cyborg dimensions” of consumer behavior—Extended Cognition, Hybrid Agency, Algorithmic Choice Architecture, Networked Self, Data-Driven Personalization, and Attention Governance—each grounded in posthumanist and socio-technical theory (e.g., Haraway, Simondon, Stiegler, Latour, affordance theory) and behavioral concepts (bounded rationality, nudging, social influence, attention limits). Methodologically, we adopt a conceptual research design following MacInnis (2011) and Jaakkola (2020): an interdisciplinary literature review, abductive clustering of recurring themes, iterative refinement into six analytically distinct dimensions, and illustrative mini-cases from sectors such as e-commerce, digital platforms, financial services, and health. We present an integrated conceptual model that locates the dimensions across three layers (cognitive/agency core, social–data layer, and environmental/attention layer) and relates them to consumer autonomy and market ethics. The paper concludes by outlining sector-specific implications for retailers, platforms, financial and health service providers, and regulators, and by specifying avenues for empirical research that can test and extend the Social Cyborg Consumer framework. © The Author(s) 2026.

blob: the social cyborg consumer: posthumanist framework for socio-technical consumer behavior contemporary consumers increasingly function as human–machine hybrids, challenging traditional consumer behavior models that assume a single, bounded human decision-maker. this conceptual paper introduces the social cyborg consumer framework, which integrates posthumanist philosophy of technology with mainstream consumer behavior research and behavioral economics to reconceptualize consumer choice as co-produced by human cognition and machine intelligence. building on classical decision models and digital consumer behavior research, we argue that extant theories often treat ai, algorithms, and platforms as external influences rather than as constituents of the consumer’s own decision system. we develop six socio-technical “cyborg dimensions” of consumer behavior—extended cognition, hybrid agency, algorithmic choice architecture, networked self, data-driven personalization, and attention governance—each grounded in posthumanist and socio-technical theory (e.g., haraway, simondon, stiegler, latour, affordance theory) and behavioral concepts (bounded rationality, nudging, social influence, attention limits). methodologically, we adopt a conceptual research design following macinnis (2011) and jaakkola (2020): an interdisciplinary literature review, abductive clustering of recurring themes, iterative refinement into six analytically distinct dimensions, and illustrative mini-cases from sectors such as e-commerce, digital platforms, financial services, and health. we present an integrated conceptual model that locates the dimensions across three layers (cognitive/agency core, social–data layer, and environmental/attention layer) and relates them to consumer autonomy and market ethics. the paper concludes by outlining sector-specific implications for retailers, platforms, financial and health service providers, and regulators, and by specifying avenues Abstract: Artificial intelligence is transforming how organizations assess, select, and develop talent, shifting workforce evaluation from static, retrospective criteria toward dynamic, predictive, algorithm-based models. Despite rapid technological growth, little is known about how organizational leaders interpret and use algorithmic outputs when assessing workforce value. Prior research has emphasized technology performance and adoption outcomes while overlooking the conceptual, normative, and social dimensions of decision-making at the human–algorithm interface—an omission that matters because algorithmic outputs become organizational action through meaning-making, not data processing alone. This qualitative study examined how senior leaders make sense of workforce value within AI-enabled talent management systems, focusing on the cognitive, ethical, and social dimensions of that process. Twenty-two senior leaders across four sectors (technology, finance, healthcare, and manufacturing) participated in semi-structured interviews, analyzed using a six-phase thematic analysis framework. Five interrelated themes emerged: a shift toward capability and adaptability as measures of value, tension between human judgment and algorithmic authority, ethical concerns regarding fairness, transparency, and trust, emotional and social complexities in leader decision-making, and evolving skill requirements for leading in AI-supported environments. Drawing on Sense making Theory, the findings introduce ethical mediation as a distinct, practice-based leadership construct in AI-enabled human resource management and offer recommendations for developing leader capabilities in responsible AI governance and human-centered HRM system design. © 2026 Journal of Management Practices, Humanities and Social Sciences (JMPHSS). Abstract: This article examines the main trends of information warfare and manipulations in the Ukrainian media space, as well as their influence on public opinion and democratic processes. A systematic review of 58 academic sources (2019–2025) and content analysis of 45 publications in Ukrainian media (March 2022–June 2024) were conducted using NVivo 14. In total, 1,229 coded references and 21 subthemes were recorded in both corpora. However, the analysis revealed five dominant thematic clusters: information warfare and hybrid strategies (31%), algorithmic manipulation and digital technologies of influence (22%), political communication and crisis of trust (18%), European legal and ethical responses (15%), and the Ukrainian media space as a laboratory of resilience (14%). The Ukrainian media dataset revealed five leading thematic areas: war and resistance (27%), disinformation and propaganda on Telegram (22%), reconstruction risks and corruption (19%), media literacy and fact-checking (17%), and European integration and democratic values (15%), which together reflect a gradual shift from reactive communication to proactive information security and civic empowerment. The results showed that peaks in discourse intensity coincided with critical phases of the Russian invasion, especially between March and May 2022. According to available research, Russian communication was characterized by the dominance of frames of existential threat, aggressive actor, and political criticism, the Ukrainian media corpus emphasized trust and resilience. The study also identified Ukraine as an important field of democratic resilience, where journalism, civil society, and digital media work together to counter disinformation. © The Author(s) 2026.

Title: When second-hand markets confront their ghosts: Insights from psychological reactance theory in Douala-Cameroon
Affiliations: IAE – University of Picardy Jules Verne, CRIISEA - UR UPJV, IAREMS, 3908, France; GREG-FSEGA – University of Douala, Cameroon
Authors with affiliations: Mbam A.J., IAE – University of Picardy Jules Verne, CRIISEA - UR UPJV, IAREMS, 3908, France; Choutac C., GREG-FSEGA – University of Douala, Cameroon
Abstract: The consumption of second-hand products in Douala (Cameroon) unfolds within a fragile equilibrium shaped by informal market dynamics, social norms, and culturally embedded representations. Drawing on participant observations and semi-structured interviews, this study shows that second-hand purchasing extends far beyond an economic decision. Technical uncertainty, social stigma, culturally rooted beliefs about the prior use of objects, and the lack of clear legal protections structure consumers’ hesitations. These barriers do not merely generate avoidance: they activate psychological reactance when individuals perceive that their freedom of choice is constrained whether by economic necessity, social expectations, or moral judgments and seek to restore autonomy while navigating community norms and symbolic risks. The findings extend psychological reactance theory by demonstrating that, in the informal markets of Douala, reactance arises not only from prescriptive messages but also from structural constraints, status-based evaluations, and culturally grounded interpretations of risk. Reactance is simultaneously shaped by spiritual beliefs, tensions between modern and traditional consumption norms, and collective narratives circulating within peer groups. Trust in sellers, products, and informal guarantees, as well as perceived value economic, social, and symbolic emerge as key levers for reducing reactance. The study offers context-specific managerial implications, including reframing second-hand purchasing as a competent and legitimate choice, strengthening local trust-building practices, developing non-prescriptive and culturally sensitive communication, and supporting informal markets through proportionate mechanisms that reduce risk without limiting consumer autonomy. © 2026 The Author(s). Title: Consumer interest protection in unfair competition in the digital economy era
Affiliations: Binary Graduate School, Ioi Business Park, NO. 1, Selangor, Puchong, 47100, Malaysia
Authors with affiliations: Liu F., Binary Graduate School, Ioi Business Park, NO. 1, Selangor, Puchong, 47100, Malaysia; Li Z., Binary Graduate School, Ioi Business Park, NO. 1, Selangor, Puchong, 47100, Malaysia
Abstract: This study explores the protection of consumer interests in the context of unfair competition in the digital economy. With the rapid development of digital technology, the role and status of consumers in the market have changed significantly, and consumers are not only the receivers of goods and services but also the suppliers of new production factors. However, operators' unfair competition behaviors, such as algorithmic manipulation and big data exploitation, have seriously damaged consumers' rights to know, choose, and welfare. This study analyzes the transformation of unfair competition behavior and its causes, points out the deficiencies of the current law in the protection of consumer interests, and proposes a transformation path from passive protection to active protection, indirect protection to direct protection, and individual protection to collective protection. Finally, this paper offers suggestions on system construction from three aspects: perfecting legal rules, strengthening judicial protection, and optimizing auxiliary mechanisms, in order to comprehensively enhance the protection of consumer interests. © 2025 by the authors; licensee Learning Gate.

Title: Saving Sade: Monstrosity, Theology, and Our Impasse in Algorithmic Culture
Affiliations: University of Helsinki, Finland
Authors with affiliations: Botez A., University of Helsinki, Finland; Hietanen J., University of Helsinki, Finland
Abstract: We are fascinated by the abnormal, transgressive, and irresolvable. Apart from zombies and other horrific tropes, there are also literary figures that are both obscene and enticing. We focus on the Marquis de Sade, whose macabre fictions continue to resonate in contemporary culture. We argue that various reactions to Sade’s texts are marked by an irreducible embeddedness in Christian culture. This tends to lead into a focus on his fictitious excesses and attempts to explain and resolve his aberrance. In contrast, we read Sade theologically to reveal a radical attempt to return to the Hellenistic worldview of fearsome purity and the absolute essences overturned by Christianity. Title: “How do we do that?” An analysis of TikToks by lesbians over age 30 representing sexual identity, lived experience over time, and solidarity
Affiliations: Concordia University, Montreal, QC, Canada
Authors with affiliations: Jamet-Lange H., Concordia University, Montreal, QC, Canada; Duguay S., Concordia University, Montreal, QC, Canada
Abstract: Lesbians have long turned to digital media and technologies for information, support, and to self-represent sexual identity in ways that have the capacity for building communities and gathering publics and counterpublics. TikTok is a short video platform popular with young people, which has increasingly seen the participation of comparatively older users. This paper investigates the self-representation of lesbians over age 30 on TikTok to understand the themes in their content and how the platform shapes their communication with others. Through sampling tailored to TikTok’s algorithmic curation, ten lesbians’ accounts are examined alongside qualitative coding and analysis of 50 of these creators’ videos. Findings reveal key themes regarding the expression of identity and age, lived experience over time, and bids for connection and community. TikTokers expressed lesbian identity in continuity with longstanding stereotypes to enhance visibility but also incorporated humor and youthful trends to give rise to novel identity expressions. Videos showcasing the passage of time and sociopolitical change demonstrated the resilience of lesbian lives and conveyed hope while advice and statements of solidarity expressed support for young people’s present struggles with homophobia and transphobia. Contrasting with studies of TikTok’s generational wars, this article shows how older lesbians are building generational bridges through their uptake of youth-driven platform practices, sharing of past challenges to support youth in overcoming present hurdles, and by modeling lesbian futures. © 2024 Taylor & Francis Group, LLC.

Title: Echo chambers
Source title: Elgar Encyclopedia of Political Communication: Volume 1-3
Affiliations: University of Antwerp, Belgium
Authors with affiliations: Terren L., University of Antwerp, Belgium
Abstract: In the last decades, the metaphor of “echo chambers” gained prominence in the context of online and social media communication. It refers to (online) spaces in which pre-existing beliefs and values are repeated and reinforced, exposing users to increasingly similar content while shielding them from more diverse and alternative viewpoints. Echo chambers are believed to stem from our tendency to interact with like-minded others, and to be facilitated by online algorithms. Although echo chambers can exist offline, technological developments and a high-choice media environment can reinforce segregation on a larger scale. Looking for evidence of echo chambers online, empirical studies have yielded mixed results, with some studies finding clear evidence of echo chambers on social media and others finding – on the contrary – evidence of cross-cutting interactions and exposure. A better understanding of this phenomenon is crucial to addressing its potential consequences, namely increasing polarization and the amplification of mis- and disinformation. © The Editors and Contributors Severally 2025.

Title: Digital Marketing and Artificial Intelligence
Affiliations: University of Cambridge Judge Business School, Cambridge, United Kingdom
Authors with affiliations: Romic J., University of Cambridge Judge Business School, Cambridge, United Kingdom
Abstract: In recent years Artificial Intelligence (AI) has come to represent a transformative force in several fields, including digital marketing. Specifically, digital marketing augmented by AI has drastically reoriented how firms create context, manage consumer experiences and expectations, and generate novel revenue opportunities. With the introduction and integration of AI in digital marketing, firms can analyze and collate enormous amounts of data, enabling them to recognize market and consumer patterns and improve their decision-making processes. These capabilities have revolutionized the digital marketing industry and significantly altered the way firms engage and interact with their customers and the environment. Although these capabilities present profound opportunities for firms, the full breadth of the potential impacts and applications of AI in digital marketing has not yet reached maturity. Several factors inhibit the full deployment of these emerging capabilities. For example, the development of the necessary human capital in conjunction with building sufficient domain proficiency. Moreover, these expanded capabilities have introduced several ethical concerns and legal risks, including the potential to manipulate or influence consumer purchasing decisions, consumer autonomy, and the adequacy of existing consumer privacy rights. Moving forward firms must walk a delicate balance between seizing emerging opportunities and ensuring the ethical protection of consumers and the autonomy of their individual decisions. © 2026 Elsevier Inc. Abstract: Despite the rapid expansion of AI technology in digital communication, this study analyzes how AI shapes political communication in Southeast Asia. The primary focus is on how AI creates, distributes, and improves emotionally charged and manipulative political content and how it affects political polarisation in Indonesia, Malaysia, and Thailand. This mixed-methods inquiry analyzes the utilization of AI in digital public spheres through a combination of public opinion surveys, automated analysis of social media sentiment, interviews, and analysis of digital discourse. The majority of participants reported strong emotional responses towards political information produced by AI, particularly regarding religion and ethnicity. Interviews and discourse analysis revealed that political actors can imply the use of AI technology to polarise public opinion or create negative discourse on social media. This paper contains integrations of affect Theory, algorithmic agency, and digital political communication. The results of this study highlight the need for improved digital literacy and emotional intelligence to address the potential for affective engineering in political contexts driven by AI. In addition, this study opens up future opportunities for additional study into similarly constructed social forces of resistance that could combat algorithmically driven political content across digital public spheres within democratic settings. © 2026 The Authors.

Title: Driving Service Stickiness in the AI Subscription Economy: The Roles of Algorithmic Curation, Technological Fluidity, and Cognitive Efficiency

Authors with affiliations: Kim B., Department of Business Administration, Hanyang University, Seoul, 04763, South Korea; Park J., ABH DXIAI LAB, 1113, Busan, 48092, South Korea
Abstract: This study examines the psychological mechanisms underlying service stickiness during the mature phase of the AI subscription economy, with particular attention to the paradox of subscription fatigue. To enhance conceptual clarity, AI-driven stimuli—specifically Algorithmic Curation and Technological Fluidity—are defined as perceived attributes at the individual level. Employing the Stimulus–Organism–Response (S-O-R) framework, the research explores how these perceived stimuli influence consumers’ internal states (Cognitive Efficiency and Serendipity) and subsequent behavioral responses (Service Stickiness). Empirical analysis using partial least squares structural equation modeling (PLS-SEM) on data from U.S. subscription service users yields several theoretical insights. Cognitive Efficiency is identified as the primary driver of stickiness, indicating that, in the context of subscription fatigue, the utilitarian benefit of reduced cognitive effort surpasses hedonic enjoyment. Additionally, the study identifies a “Frictionless Trap,” in which excessive Technological Fluidity negatively affects Serendipity (β = −0.195), suggesting that an entirely seamless experience may create a filter bubble that limits unexpected discovery. As a result, Serendipity does not significantly affect stickiness in the aggregate model. However, post hoc analysis demonstrates that Serendipity remains significant for high-income users, while Cognitive Efficiency is most influential in high-frequency utilitarian contexts, such as food services. These findings indicate that sustainable retention depends on reducing cognitive load while intentionally introducing friction to preserve opportunities for discovery. © 2026 by the authors.

blob: driving service stickiness in the ai subscription economy: the roles of algorithmic curation, technological fluidity, and cognitive efficiency this study examines the psychological mechanisms underlying service stickiness during the mature phase of the ai subscription economy, with particular attention to the paradox of subscription fatigue. to enhance conceptual clarity, ai-driven stimuli—specifically algorithmic curation and technological fluidity—are defined as perceived attributes at the individual level. employing the stimulus–organism–response (s-o-r) framework, the research explores how these perceived stimuli influence consumers’ internal states (cognitive efficiency and serendipity) and subsequent behavioral responses (service stickiness). empirical analysis using partial least squares structural equation modeling (pls-sem) on data from u.s. subscription service users yields several theoretical insights. cognitive efficiency is identified as the primary driver of stickiness, indicating that, in the context of subscription fatigue, the utilitarian benefit of reduced cognitive effort surpasses hedonic enjoyment. additionally, the study identifies a “frictionless trap,” in which excessive technological fluidity negatively affects serendipity (β = −0.195), suggesting that an entirely seamless experience may create a filter bubble that limits unexpected discovery. as a result, serendipity does not significantly affect stickiness in the aggregate model. however, post hoc analysis demonstrates that serendipity remains significant for high-income users, while cognitive efficiency is most influential in high-frequency utilitarian contexts, such as food services. these findings indicate that sustainable retention depends on reducing cognitive load while intentionally introducing friction to preserve opportunities for discovery. © 2026 by the authors. ai subscription economy; Abstract: As artificial intelligence (AI) shifts from experimental novelty to a ubiquitous commercial driver, its integration into marketing has outpaced robust regulatory development. This chapter investigates the intersection of innovation and oversight. While AI enables unprecedented hyper-personalization, it introduces systemic risks including algorithmic bias, consumer autonomy, and black-box decision-making. This study identifies critical policy gaps where current legislation fails to match technological velocity. By evaluating three primary regulatory paths: Precautionary, Market-Driven, and State-Centric, the discussion advocates for harmonized governance that secures digital sovereignty without stifling growth. It proposes a multi-layered mechanism combining institutional ethics boards, technical explainability, and market-based audits. Ultimately, this work provides a strategic roadmap to align AI commercialization with human-centric values, ensuring trust remains the primary currency of the digital marketplace. Abstract: This chapter examines how algorithmic authority is reshaping organisational life and workforce strategies, and its implications for human resilience. Moving beyond deterministic views of automation, algorithmic authority is a contingent arrangement shaped by governance and worker agency. Evidence from healthcare, law, & HRM indicates “centaur models” of human–AI collaboration achieve efficiency while preserving accountability. Scenario analysis for 2030 projects three models: augmentation-dominant, automation-heavy, and hybrid adaptive, each with distinct risks, opportunities, & resilience strategies. Linking these scenarios to the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs), mainly SDG 8, 5 & 9, the chapter highlights that human-centric AI integration can support equity and sustainability. A conceptual framework integrates algorithmic authority, resilience, and sustainable futures, showing how human-in-the-loop design, fairness audits, and participatory governance can transform disruption into inclusion. It concludes with implications for theory, practice, policy, and future research agenda. Copyright © 2027, IGI Global Scientific Publishing. Abstract: The rise of digital streaming platforms is transforming cinema culture in technological and power relations contexts. Algorithmic curation on Netflix, Disney+ and Amazon Prime Video shapes preferences and restructures circulation, challenging theideaofthe“free-choosingindividual.”Thisstudyexamineshowrecommendation systems shape viewer subjectivity in film culture. Visibility is shaped by data-driven feeds based on viewing history, clicks and interaction data. It asks whether viewers choose, whether algorithms shape taste, and whether genres are constructed algorithmically. It argues cultural preferences are shaped by class habitus and data classification systems. Methodologically, the study uses critical theory on platform capitalism, surveillance and cultural studies. Title: From Automation to Agency: Distributed Algorithmic Authority in Physical AI-Enabled Warehouse Execution Systems
Affiliations: Faculty of Economics and Business, University of Maribor, Maribor, 2000, Slovenia
Authors with affiliations: Logožar K., Faculty of Economics and Business, University of Maribor, Maribor, 2000, Slovenia
Abstract: (1) Background: Physical artificial intelligence is progressing beyond performing tasks. As embodied AI systems integrate sensing, context-sensitive inference, orchestration, and physical actuation, the central issue shifts from automation efficiency to the redistribution of decision authority within organizational execution. (2) Methods: This paper develops a conceptual systems framework through structured, problem-centered conceptual theorizing. It integrates organizational information processing theory, requisite-variety and viable-system reasoning, near-decomposability and interactive-complexity perspectives, human-factors research, organizational authority, and socio-technical systems theory. (3) Results: The framework conceptualizes physical AI as a facility-level socio-technical execution architecture and introduces distributed algorithmic authority (DAA) as the degree to which real operational decision authority is distributed across interacting human, algorithmic, and embodied components. DAA comprises four dimensions: the scope of delegated decision rights, the locus and distribution of authority, revocability and intervention rights, and decision legibility. The framework distinguishes DAA intensity from DAA controllability and proposes an inverted-U relationship between DAA intensity and facility-level system performance. Greater DAA intensity can improve local responsiveness while eventually reducing coordination coherence and corrective control when the variety of distributed decisions exceeds the architecture’s coordinating capacity. DAA controllability and system-level control capacity—comprising governance maturity, coordinating variety, intervention capacity, and data integrity—shift the viable threshold of distributed authority. (4) Conclusions: Physical AI should be understood not simply as an automation capability, but as a socio-technical reconfiguration of execution and control whose effects depend on whether distributed operational authority remains legible, revocable, and governable at the system level. © 2026 by the author.

blob: from automation to agency: distributed algorithmic authority in physical ai-enabled warehouse execution systems (1) background: physical artificial intelligence is progressing beyond performing tasks. as embodied ai systems integrate sensing, context-sensitive inference, orchestration, and physical actuation, the central issue shifts from automation efficiency to the redistribution of decision authority within organizational execution. (2) methods: this paper develops a conceptual systems framework through structured, problem-centered conceptual theorizing. it integrates organizational information processing theory, requisite-variety and viable-system reasoning, near-decomposability and interactive-complexity perspectives, human-factors research, organizational authority, and socio-technical systems theory. (3) results: the framework conceptualizes physical ai as a facility-level socio-technical execution architecture and introduces distributed algorithmic authority (daa) as the degree to which real operational decision authority is distributed across interacting human, algorithmic, and embodied components. daa comprises four dimensions: the scope of delegated decision rights, the locus and distribution of authority, revocability and intervention rights, and decision legibility. the framework distinguishes daa intensity from daa controllability and proposes an inverted-u relationship between daa intensity and facility-level system performance. greater daa intensity can improve local responsiveness while eventually reducing coordination coherence and corrective control when the variety of distributed decisions exceeds the architecture’s coordinating capacity. daa controllability and system-level control capacity—comprising governance maturity, coordinating variety, intervention capacity, and data integrity—shift the viable threshold of distributed authority. Abstract: This study presents the analysis of intellectual property rights for product designers, which may be used to advance environmentally friendly product designs while preserving consumer autonomy and environmental sustainability. This study presents whether or not these rights might serve as a motivator for the creation and adoption of environmentally friendly product designs and sustainable practices. A better knowledge of Industry 5.0 may contribute to sustainable development anticipated from Industry 5.0-driven sustainability development. Functions should be managed to maximise their synergies and contribution to the intended sustainability values. Title: Misinformation, disinformation, and fake news
Affiliations: Northern Illinois University, DeKalb, IL, United States
Authors with affiliations: Wright M.F., Northern Illinois University, DeKalb, IL, United States
Abstract: This chapter explores the complex issues of misinformation, disinformation, and fake news, which have become significant challenges in the digital age. It examines the definitions and characteristics of these phenomena, emphasizing their role in shaping public discourse, political polarization, and undermining trust in media and institutions. The chapter highlights how the rise of social media, automated bots, and algorithmic manipulation have amplified the spread of false information, making it more difficult to distinguish fact from fiction. It also considers the psychological and social factors that contribute to the widespread acceptance and dissemination of fake news, such as cognitive biases and emotional triggers. The chapter discusses current efforts to combat misinformation, including fact-checking, automated detection systems, and media literacy initiatives. Finally, it underscores the importance of a multidimensional approach to addressing these issues, one that involves technological solutions, educational strategies, and fostering critical thinking to strengthen the integrity of public information. © Editor and Contributors Severally 2025.

Title: HOW SOCIAL MEDIA CONTRIBUTE TO DEMOCRATIC EROSION
Source title: The Routledge Companion to Digital Media and Democracy
Affiliations: Department of Journalism, Media and Communication, University of Gothenburg, Sweden; Department of Journalism, Media and Communication, University of Gothenburg, Sweden
Authors with affiliations: Strömbäck J., Department of Journalism, Media and Communication, University of Gothenburg, Sweden; Åkerlund M., Department of Journalism, Media and Communication, University of Gothenburg, Sweden
Abstract: Despite early optimism that social media would invigorate democratic processes, it has instead coincided with a process of democratic erosion. Still, research on the connection between these remains scattered. This chapter seeks to remedy this through an analysis of how social media contribute to democratic erosion by facilitating and amplifying disinformation, anti-democratic, and illiberal discourses. The chapter highlights four key ways whereby social media contribute to democratic erosion: the absence of gatekeeping, by allowing anonymity, by following a follower logic, and through algorithmic curation. These functions, in turn, facilitate the spread and prevalence of anti-democratic, illiberal and hateful discourse, the spread and prevalence of false and misleading information, the forming of inward-facing spaces attracting those who hold the most anti-democratic and illiberal views, and enable expressions of anti-democratic and illiberal discourse to seep into outward-facing digital and mainstream media. These problems are further exacerbated by the unwillingness of social media companies to engage in thorough moderation, and probably by the increasing importance of generative AI. © 2026 selection and editorial matter, Zizi Papacharissi; individual chapters, the contributors.

Abstract: Media messages shape our knowledge about the world, but measuring individual exposure and attention remains challenging. Emerging media offer a solution to studying message reception in simulated real-world environments, which may soon become the actual media environments in which we encounter messages. Here, we utilized virtual reality (VR) and eye-tracking to investigate message processing in a realistic virtual city environment populated with billboards. We introduced an inception-style manipulation where billboards initially overlooked by participants were covertly reintroduced based on real-time gaze tracking. Our findings show this algorithmic manipulation, undetected by participants, significantly boosted message memory retention for the targeted messages. This study reveals a path of media influence, demonstrating how undetected algorithmic manipulations can shape individual and collective memory. The findings carry practical and theoretical implications for diverse communication contexts, from advertising and public health to political messaging in the emerging metaverse ecosystem. © The Author(s) 2025. blob: memory inception through gaze-contingent message exposure: using virtual reality to study media influence media messages shape our knowledge about the world, but measuring individual exposure and attention remains challenging. emerging media offer a solution to studying message reception in simulated real-world environments, which may soon become the actual media environments in which we encounter messages. here, we utilized virtual reality (vr) and eye-tracking to investigate message processing in a realistic virtual city environment populated with billboards. we introduced an inception-style manipulation where billboards initially overlooked by participants were covertly reintroduced based on real-time gaze tracking. our findings show this algorithmic manipulation, undetected by participants, significantly boosted message memory retention for the targeted messages. this study reveals a path of media influence, demonstrating how undetected algorithmic manipulations can shape individual and collective memory. the findings carry practical and theoretical implications for diverse communication contexts, from advertising and public health to political messaging in the emerging metaverse ecosystem. © the author(s) 2025. published by oxford university press on behalf of international communication association. all rights reserved. for commercial re-use, please contact reprints@oup.com for reprints and translation rights for reprints. all other permissions can be obtained through our rightslink service via the permissions link on the article page on our site—for further information please contact journals.permissions@oup.com. this article is published and distributed under the terms of the oxford university press, standard journals publication model (https://academic.oup.com/pages/standard-publication-reuse-rights)  algorithm; communication; memory; multimedia; perception; public attitude; virtual reality

Title: Surveillance, Suggestion, and Sabotage: Understanding Consumer Pushback Against AI in E-Commerce and Q-Commerce
Affiliations: School of Business, Woxsen University, Hyderabad, India; Symbiosis International (Deemed University), Pune, India; Keele Business School, Keele University, Staffordshire, United Kingdom
Authors with affiliations: Pahari S., School of Business, Woxsen University, Hyderabad, India; Patra M., Symbiosis International (Deemed University), Pune, India; Oyenuga M.O., School of Business, Woxsen University, Hyderabad, India; Mogaji E., Keele Business School, Keele University, Staffordshire, United Kingdom
Abstract: This research explored the psychological and behavioral resistance of consumers toward AI-enabled personalization in the contexts of e-commerce and quick commerce (Q-commerce). Though advanced AI technologies offer benefits such as efficiency and convenience, consumers report concerns about emotional manipulation, information overload, and diminished consumer autonomy. Using the Technology Threat Avoidance Theory (TTAT) and the Stimulus–Organism–Behavior–Consequence (SOBC) model, we have explained how AI-related stimuli may evoke consumer resistance. We used a mixed-methods approach. In Study 1, we conducted in-depth interviews with 18 Indian consumers to identify the dominant factors of resistance, and in Study 2, we surveyed 487 consumers. We validated and tested the proposed framework using Confirmatory Factor Analysis (CFA) and structural equation modelling (SEM). Findings show that emotional manipulation and information overload increase consumers' threat perception of AI and psychological reactance. These, in turn, lead to resistance intentions, platform avoidance, and brand distrust. However, brands' CSR initiatives and human oversight throughout the process can weaken the relationship between resistance behaviors and brand distrust. In short, our findings suggest that consumer resistance to AI is a patterned response to emotional and ethical concerns- not a direct rejection of AI. This study provides helpful insights for managers, designers, and policymakers to develop more transparent and responsible AI systems in the context of e-commerce and Q-commerce. © 2026 John Wiley & Sons Ltd.

Title: How social media affordances shape journalistic content production: A stimulus-based interview study on journalists’ perceptions
Affiliations: LMU Munich, Germany
Authors with affiliations: Anter L., LMU Munich, Germany
Abstract: Social media platforms are increasingly central for delivering journalistic content. While evidence suggests that social media led to adaptations of journalistic production routines, comparatively little is known about the specific platform characteristics that shape coordinating, selecting, and editing social media content. Adopting an affordance lens, this study seeks to tackle this gap and investigates how social media journalists perceive platform properties and their influence on journalistic contenft production. To answer this question, the study relies on stimulus-based qualitative interviews with 34 social media journalists from Germany, focusing primarily on TikTok, Instagram, and Facebook. By combining platform walkthroughs and reconstruction interviews, the analysis provides fine-grained insights into how a set of affordances, ranging from the perceived degree of algorithmic curation over (user-induced) spatiotemporal boundaries to platforms’ communicative forms, shapes the different stages of content production. The proposed affordances are both universal and variable, forming a typology that facilitates systematic comparisons across current and future platforms. © The Author(s) 2025. Title: News content promotion pressure: A content analysis of the cross-media visibility of and engagement with news stories
Affiliations: Vrije Universiteit Amsterdam, Netherlands; University of Antwerp, Belgium
Authors with affiliations: Lamot K., Vrije Universiteit Amsterdam, Netherlands; Paulussen S., University of Antwerp, Belgium
Abstract: The research at hand centered around examining how news media manage their visibility, while navigating the challenges of invisibility posed by the platform economy. Platforms shape the visibility of news organizations and their content through algorithmic curation and moderation. In response, news organizations must exert considerable effort to maximize their visibility within these systems. The research identified and analyzed various deliberate promotional strategies aimed at enhancing an article’s visibility, including strategic posting across platforms, homepage placement, and extending content lifespan. By aggregating these strategies into a “promotion pressure” score, the study aims to unravel the circular relationship between news media’s content promotion strategies and audience engagement with news stories. Further analysis of the news articles with the highest promotion pressure shows that they are mostly related to major events, rely on news values such as conflict and personification, and frequently use clickbait headlines. © The Author(s) 2024. Title: Taming TikTok: how BIPOC individuals perceive and interact with algorithmically generated content
Affiliations: University of Wisconsin-Madison, United States; UT Austin, United States; Information College, University of Maryland, College Park, United States; School of Information, The University of Texas at Austin, United States
Authors with affiliations: Dai J., University of Wisconsin-Madison, United States; Hajiyeva N., UT Austin, United States; Wan S., Information College, University of Maryland, College Park, United States; Booth K., School of Information, The University of Texas at Austin, United States
Abstract: Introduction. TikTok’s recommendation algorithm plays a crucial role in shaping user experiences, raising concerns about algorithmic bias, content suppression, and misinformation, particularly for BIPOC users. This study explores how BIPOC individuals perceive and interact with TikTok’s algorithm, focusing on content visibility, algorithmic manipulation, and experiences with problematic content. Method. This pilot study utilized semi-structured interviews with 10 BIPOC TikTok users, recruited via social media. Participants discussed their experiences with the platform’s recommendation system, and responses were transcribed and thematically analyzed to identify patterns in content exposure, engagement strategies, and perceptions of algorithmic bias. Analysis. A qualitative thematic coding approach was applied to categorize responses based on key themes, including content representation, misinformation, and strategies for mitigating algorithmic harm. Results. Findings reveal that BIPOC users frequently encounter discriminatory content, misinformation, and algorithmic suppression. Many employ strategies such as selective engagement, the "Not Interested" feature, and algorithm resets to curate their feed. However, skepticism remains regarding TikTok’s data practices and fairness in content moderation. Conclusions. BIPOC users actively shape their digital experiences to counteract algorithmic bias, highlighting systemic inequities in AI-driven platforms. Future research should expand participant diversity and investigate long-term algorithmic trends to promote inclusive digital spaces. © The Author(s).

Title: Comics as Heritage: Theorizing Digital Futures of Vernacular Expression
Affiliations: Department of ALM (Archives, Library and Information Science Museum and Cultural Heritage Studies), Centre for Digital Humanities and Social Sciences (CDHU), Uppsala University, P.O. Box 256, Uppsala, SE-751 05, Sweden
Authors with affiliations: Manouach I.; Foka A., Department of ALM (Archives, Library and Information Science Museum and Cultural Heritage Studies), Centre for Digital Humanities and Social Sciences (CDHU), Uppsala University, P.O. Box 256, Uppsala, SE-751 05, Sweden
Abstract: This paper investigates digital comics—particularly webcomics and webtoons—as emerging forms of cultural heritage, analyzing their exponential global influence alongside the limitations of traditional heritage frameworks in systematically preserving them. The UNESCO heritage model, rooted in concepts of physical fixity and authenticity, is shown as inadequate for born-digital works like comics, which derive meaning from technological infrastructure, dynamic platforms, and ongoing community interaction rather than static material forms. Drawing on heritage futures and digital materiality theories, the authors argue that digital comics exemplify "temporal authenticity," evolving through continual transformation and algorithmic curation. The paper details how platform recommendation systems and analytics directly shape which comics achieve cultural visibility and preservation, while community-driven initiatives—such as The Flashpoint Archive—demonstrate effective models for holistic, grassroots digital preservation beyond institutional reach. Ultimately, the study calls for new theoretical and practical approaches to heritage, recognizing digital comics as both cultural artifacts and dynamic, platform-specific vernacular expressions. © 2025 by the authors.
